question: My freight arrived damaged. Who do I claim against, and how long do I have?
aliases: how long do I have to file a freight claim
Carmack Amendment 9 month claim filing deadline
who is liable for cargo damage interline shipment
carrier has not responded to my cargo claim 120 days
shortAnswer: Read the bill of lading for the deadline, because the statute sets a floor rather than a date: a carrier may provide no less than 9 months for filing a claim and no less than 2 years for bringing a civil action [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. As for who, liability reaches the receiving carrier, the delivering carrier, and any carrier over whose line or route the property was transported [S:usc-49-14706-carmack], and the claim may be filed with the receiving or delivering carrier, the carrier that issued the bill of lading, or the carrier on whose line the loss occurred [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii]. One trap before anything else: a communication is only treated as a claim if it identifies the shipment, asserts liability, and claims payment of a specified or determinable amount of money [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii].
assumes: You are asking about interstate motor carriage governed by the federal framework. This record holds no state regulation of intrastate carriage, which is a separate body of law, and whether a purely intrastate move is governed by any of this should be settled first.
You are asking what the law requires rather than what your policy pays. Nothing here states what any cargo policy covers, and cargo forms are not publicly filed.

You are reading the statute on the official host and the regulations from a reproduction. Section 14706 is quoted from the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's own site [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]; the three regulations are quoted from Cornell's Legal Information Institute because the official eCFR did not serve at the time of access [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii][S:cfr-49-370-9-lii][S:cfr-49-387-303-lii].
why:
Start with the thing that ends more freight claims than any argument about who damaged what: the claim was never a claim.

A written or electronic communication is treated as a claim only where it contains facts sufficient to identify the shipment, asserts liability for the alleged loss, damage, injury or delay, and makes claim for the payment of a specified or determinable amount of money [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii]. Three elements, together. The third is the one that is usually missing, because the natural first move is to send photographs and a description while the amount is still being worked out. The regulation is explicit that bad order reports, appraisal reports of damage and similar documents shall, standing alone, not be considered by carriers as sufficient to comply with the minimum claim filing requirements [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii], and it requires a formal claim in writing for a specified or determinable amount of money before voluntary payment [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii]. So a file of correspondence can accumulate for months while nothing that counts has been filed, and the period keeps running.

Now the period, and this is where most published answers give a number that is not the answer. Section 14706(e) does not impose a deadline. It sets floors on what a carrier may provide: no less than 9 months for filing a claim, and no less than 2 years for bringing a civil action [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. The operative period is the one written into the bill of lading, and it cannot be shorter than these. Nine months is therefore the shortest the deadline can lawfully be, not the deadline itself, and the document that tells you which it is arrived with the freight.

Which brings up the bill of lading generally, because it does more work here than the policy does. A carrier must issue a receipt or bill of lading for property it receives for transportation, and failure to issue one does not affect the carrier's liability [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. That last clause is worth holding onto: a missing bill of lading is a problem of proof, not a defence.

Then who. The instinct is to pursue whoever damaged the goods, and on an interlined move that may be the hardest fact to establish. The statute does not require you to establish it first. Liability attaches to the actual loss or injury to the property caused by the receiving carrier, the delivering carrier, or another carrier over whose line or route the property is transported [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. So who caused the loss and who can be liable are separate questions, and a delivering carrier can answer for damage that happened before it took the trailer.

The filing rule matches that. A claim goes to the receiving or delivering carrier, the carrier issuing the bill of lading, receipt, ticket or baggage check, or the carrier on whose line the alleged loss, damage, injury or delay occurred, within the applicable time limits [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii]. And if it goes to suit, an action may be brought against the delivering carrier in a district or state court where that carrier operates, or against the carrier alleged to have caused the loss in the district where the loss occurred [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. On a multi-carrier move that is a choice, and it is worth making deliberately.

What happens after you file is also regulated, which surprises people who have been waiting. A carrier must pay, decline, or make a firm compromise settlement offer in writing within 120 days after receipt of the claim [S:cfr-49-370-9-lii]. Where it cannot dispose of the claim in that time, it must advise the claimant in writing at the expiration of each succeeding 60-day period of the status of the claim and the reason for the delay [S:cfr-49-370-9-lii]. Silence for a year is not one of the permitted outcomes.

And that duty connects to the second clock in a way that is easy to miss. The 2-year period for bringing a civil action runs from the date the carrier gives written notice that it has disallowed any part of the claim [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. The start of the period is established by a document the carrier produces. So where no written disposition has ever arrived, both sides are holding a file whose limitation date nobody can state, and the 120-day duty is precisely the obligation that is supposed to produce that document [S:cfr-49-370-9-lii]. Asking for the written decline is not just chasing an answer; it is fixing a date.

On how much, two sentences do most of the work. The measure is the actual loss or injury to the property [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. But a carrier may establish rates under which its liability is limited to a value established by written or electronic declaration of the shipper, or by written agreement between carrier and shipper, if that value would be reasonable under the circumstances [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. A declared or released value on the bill of lading is therefore the first thing to look for, and the reasonableness condition is part of the provision rather than a gloss on it. For household goods there is a more generous default: maximum liability is replacement value up to the declared value, unless a waiver is provided in writing [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].

One last thing, because it is the most common false comfort on this subject. Being told a carrier meets its federal insurance requirements says nothing about the freight. The cargo minimum in the federal rules is five thousand dollars for loss of or damage to household goods carried on any one motor vehicle and ten thousand dollars for the aggregate at any one time and place, and it applies to household goods motor carriers alone [S:cfr-49-387-303-lii]. There is no federal cargo insurance minimum stated for a general freight carrier, and the section provides that carriers subject to its minimum limits are at no time required to hold security for more than those minimums [S:cfr-49-387-303-lii]. The large federal figures, from three hundred thousand dollars to five million, are public liability minimums for bodily injury and property damage, which is a different exposure from the goods on the trailer [S:cfr-49-387-303-lii].
whatChanges: What period the bill of lading actually provides, since the statute sets floors of 9 months and 2 years rather than the deadline itself [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Whether what you sent meets all three claim elements, in particular whether it claimed a specified or determinable amount of money [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii].
Whether the move was interlined, because liability reaches any carrier over whose line or route the property was transported [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Whether a declared or released value appears on the bill of lading, which is how a limitation of liability is created [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Whether the carrier has given written notice disallowing any part of the claim, since that is what starts the 2-year period [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Whether the shipment was household goods, which carries a replacement-value default and a written-waiver requirement [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Whether the carriage was interstate, since this record establishes nothing about intrastate motor carriage.
variability: Section 14706 is quoted from the preliminary edition on the official host [S:usc-49-14706-carmack]. The three regulations are quoted from a reproduction on Cornell's Legal Information Institute rather than the official eCFR, which served a bot-detection page rather than the regulation at the time of access [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii][S:cfr-49-370-9-lii][S:cfr-49-387-303-lii]. Anything that matters to a decision should be read against the official text.

This record sets out 49 CFR 370.3 and 370.9 only. The acknowledgment requirement in 370.5, the investigation requirement in 370.7 and the salvage provisions in 370.11 were not read, and nothing here establishes their contents [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii][S:cfr-49-370-9-lii].

Whether a limitation of liability holds is not settled by the existence of a declared value. The provision applies where that value would be reasonable under the circumstances [S:usc-49-14706-carmack], which is a question decided on the facts and not by this page.

Nothing here establishes what any cargo policy covers, whether any particular claim is payable, or what a court would find about where a loss occurred. Cargo forms are not publicly filed and this record has read none.
The dollar figures in the federal security minimums have been revised over the life of the part and are stated here as at the access date [S:cfr-49-387-303-lii].
nextActions: Find the bill of lading and read the claim and suit periods off it before calendaring anything, since the statute only sets floors [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
File something that satisfies all three elements at once, including a specified or determinable amount of money, rather than sending photographs and a description and waiting [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii].

Decide which carrier to file with, given that the receiving carrier, the delivering carrier, the carrier that issued the bill of lading and the carrier on whose line the loss occurred are all named [S:cfr-49-370-3-lii][S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
Check the bill of lading for a declared or released value, because that is where a limitation on the actual loss measure comes from [S:usc-49-14706-carmack].
If 120 days have passed with no written disposition, ask for one in writing and cite the obligation, since the carrier owes a written status every 60 days after that as well [S:cfr-49-370-9-lii].

Do not treat a carrier's federal filing as cargo cover. Ask what cargo limit the carrier actually holds, because the federal cargo minimum reaches household goods carriers only [S:cfr-49-387-303-lii].
author: Aaron Bollinger

handoff.reason: Whether a limitation of liability holds, which carrier to pursue on an interlined move, and whether a communication already filed counts as a claim are all decided on the documents and the facts. Where a filing period is close to expiring this is time-critical and belongs with a lawyer rather than with a statute read online.
